content.overview: Civil defamation protects reputation against false and defamatory publication to a third party. Distinguish the tort from criminal defamation under BNS s. 356. Defences include truth (justification), fair comment on matters of public interest, and privilege (absolute or qualified).

sections.heading: Ingredients
sections.body: 1. Defamatory statement tending to lower the claimant in the estimation of right-thinking persons. 2. Reference to the claimant. 3. Publication to at least one third person. Libel (permanent form) and slander (spoken) are traditionally distinguished; plead the precise words and publication facts.

sections.heading: Defences
sections.body: Justification (truth of the imputations of fact). Fair comment (honest opinion on true facts on a matter of public interest). Absolute privilege (e.g. certain parliamentary and judicial occasions). Qualified privilege (duty/interest occasions, defeated by malice).

sections.heading: Track B
sections.body: Civil court suit for damages and/or injunction. Particularise the words, dates, medium, and audience. Criminal process under BNS is separate — do not conflate burden or remedy. Electronic publication still requires proof of publication and identity.

Ingredients

caseLaw.name: Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India
caseLaw.holding: The Supreme Court treated defamation by one private individual against another as a civil wrong or tort for which damages are a common-law remedy, while considering the constitutional position of reputation and free speech.
caseLaw.relevance: Directly supports the topic's treatment of civil defamation and reputation.
